Eddie Rickenbacker. The World War One fighter ace who embodied the American aviator archetype of skill, courage, and entrepreneurial spirit. Rickenbacker achieved twenty-six confirmed kills in World War One, making him America's leading ace, far ahead of his contemporaries. He flew the Spad Thirteen, a single-seat fighter aircraft that he mastered for combat operations. During the war, he survived being shot down and crashing behind enemy lines. Before the war, Rickenbacker transitioned from automobile racing, where he set speed records and won races. After the war, he became president of Eastern Air Lines, building it into a major American carrier. In nineteen forty-two, his B-17 ditched in the Pacific and he survived twenty-four days adrift, a story that became legendary. He continued his public life well into his eighties, remaining an iconic figure of American aviation. Rickenbacker was America's answer to the German ace known as the Red Baron, representing American combat prowess at the highest level. Like Jimmy Doolittle, his fellow American aviator and World War One contemporary, Rickenbacker embodied the pioneering spirit that defined aviation's golden age.
